Title: DTC P0918 - Gear Shift Position Circuit A Intermittent
Diagnostic Codes: P0918
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: Flags a gear shift position signal on circuit A that drops out or jumps for short moments in an automated manual gearbox. The module sees implausible steps or brief losses that are too short or too irregular for a lasting low or high fault. Typical triggers are terminals that lose contact under vibration, a chafed harness moving with the powertrain, or moisture at the actuator connector. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Patents from Aisin AI and Nissan/Aichi show the shift stroke sensor as the feedback that confirms an engaged gear. CARB requires circuit checks on such inputs. P0914, P0916 and P0917 are the steady electrical faults of circuit A, P0915 the plausibility fault. Shifts may abort or the gearbox may briefly fall back to neutral.
Symptoms: Warning light comes and goes; Gear changes abort now and then or the gearbox drops to neutral; Fault often appears on rough roads or in wet weather
Possible Causes: Connector at the shift sensor or actuator unit losing contact under vibration (likelihood: high); Chafed or partially broken sensor wire near the gearbox (likelihood: medium); Moisture or corrosion in the connector (likelihood: medium); Shift position sensor with an internal contact or track fault (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0918 (Gear Shift Position Circuit A Intermittent). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: gear shift position sensor a, wiring harness, tcm. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-4 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Connector at the shift sensor or actuator unit losing contact under vibration (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Chafed or partially broken sensor wire near the gearbox (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Title: DTC P2701 - Transmission Friction Element B Apply Time Range/Performance
Diagnostic Codes: P2701
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: P2701 concerns friction element B: the controller has measured an apply time for this clutch or brake that falls outside its learned window. The letter is assigned per gearbox, and bulletins show how varied the causes are. Ford's SSM 47361 pairs P2701 with P0757 on the 2018 Mustang 10R80 when it will not shift beyond second gear and traces it to one-way clutch damage in the front support. On 6F50/6F55 units built from November 2015 to February 2016, SSM 46069 and 50861 combine it with P0756 and loss of reverse, third and fifth gear, caused by a displaced direct clutch snap ring. A 2023 Stellantis case for Ram Heavy Duty trucks links P2701 and harsh shifts to a dislodged 2C clutch snap ring. Expect harsh shifts, flare or a missing gear.
Symptoms: Harsh shifts or engine flare during shifts; One or more gears missing, e.g. no upshift beyond second; Warning light on
Possible Causes: Mechanical damage in clutch B, such as a displaced snap ring or damaged hub (likelihood: high); Damaged one-way clutch working together with element B (likelihood: medium); Sticking valve or pressure control solenoid for clutch B (likelihood: medium); Low or contaminated transmission fluid (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P2701 (Transmission Friction Element B Apply Time Range/Performance). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: friction element b, hydraulic control unit, pressure control solenoid. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-12 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Mechanical damage in clutch B, such as a displaced snap ring or damaged hub (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Damaged one-way clutch working together with element B (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Problem Description: P2711 is set when the transmission controller sees the drivetrain act as if a gear were no longer properly engaged although it never commanded that, for example because a clutch drags or a gear does not engage as selected. Volkswagen Group uses it on DSG gearboxes: Audi bulletin 2029069 for the 2009-2010 A3 and TT logs it as 19143 P2711 004, with a lit gear display and shudder on the first launch, and blames a clutch that drags too strongly; VW bulletin 2028714 for 2009-2012 Jetta, Golf, CC, Eos and 2012 Passat with the 02E calls it an implausible shift sequence, caused by debris in the clutch pack, where the selected gear may not engage after start-up. Both replace the multiple clutch (beyond about 18,500 or 19,000 miles); improved clutches entered production in March 2010.
Symptoms: Gear indicator flashing or lit in the cluster; Shudder on the first drive-away; Selected Drive or Reverse does not engage after start-up
Possible Causes: Excessive drag torque in the dual clutch (worn or early-production plates) (likelihood: high); Debris inside the clutch assembly (likelihood: medium); Shift fork or gear actuator not holding the gear (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P2711 (Unexpected Mechanical Gear Disengagement). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: transmission internal, hydraulic control unit. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 4-12 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Excessive drag torque in the dual clutch (worn or early-production plates) (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Debris inside the clutch assembly (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Title: DTC P0733 - Gear 3 Incorrect Ratio
Diagnostic Codes: P0733
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: The transmission module divides input (turbine) speed by output speed and compares the result with the ratio of the commanded gear; a deviation means slip – a clutch or brake not holding, too little pressure – or a wrong gear. Thresholds: Ford more than 30 rpm off for 1.8 s three times (diesel 2023: over 20 % for 12 s), GM's 2006 tables and the Allison 1000 converter slip of 200–230 rpm for 2.25 s after one trip, Saab's Aisin boxes over 20 % twelve times without MIL. P0733 concerns third gear. Slip typically shows as flare on the 2–3 shift. If fourth or fifth gear shows the ratio of third, Aisin-type logic sets P0730 instead. Ford stores it only if the fault fits no particular solenoid. On GM manual transmissions it checks the gear position sensor.
Symptoms: Slipping or flare in third gear, engine speed higher than expected; Harsh or delayed shifts; Limp mode (Aisin: second gear and reverse only), transmission warning; Check engine light depending on manufacturer
Possible Causes: Fluid level too low or fluid worn or contaminated (likelihood: high); Clutch or brake for third gear worn (linings, piston seal) (likelihood: high); Sticking shift or pressure valve, leaking valve body gasket, blocked passages (likelihood: medium); GM manual transmissions only: gear position sensor faulty or not learned (likelihood: medium)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0733 (Gear 3 Incorrect Ratio). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: transmission clutches, transmission valve body, transmission fluid, transmission control module. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-14 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Fluid level too low or fluid worn or contaminated (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Clutch or brake for third gear worn (linings, piston seal) (likelihood: high). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Title: DTC P2E14 - Gear Selection Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
Diagnostic Codes: P2E14
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: P2E14 covers a position signal from the gear selection actuator that is present but unsteady: it drops out for moments, jumps or carries an implausible frequency or pattern, without staying low or high long enough for P2E12 or P2E13. No manufacturer documents P2E14 publicly. Two related checks show what erratic means in practice. GM's 2023 dual-clutch TCM tables reject a rod position sensor whose carrier frequency leaves the 1500 to 2500 Hz band for 150 ms (P2835, Type A). Ford's 2012 DPS6 summary watches the three Hall signals of each shift drum motor and sets P2835 if their sequence comes out of order. Loose pins, harness chafing that only touches under vibration, and electrical noise are typical. Drivers notice sporadic refused shifts or brief neutral drops that later vanish.
Symptoms: Occasional refused or delayed shifts; Short drops to neutral while driving; Warning lamp that comes and goes
Possible Causes: Loose or fretted terminal in the actuator connector (likelihood: high); Harness chafing that only shorts or opens under vibration or heat (likelihood: medium); Interference from damaged shielding or nearby motor wiring (likelihood: low); Sensor with an internal intermittent fault (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P2E14 (Gear Selection Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: gear selection actuator position sensor, wiring harness, tcm. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-5 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Loose or fretted terminal in the actuator connector (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Harness chafing that only shorts or opens under vibration or heat (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Title: DTC P0918 - Gear Shift Position Circuit A Intermittent
Diagnostic Codes: P0918
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: Flags a gear shift position signal on circuit A that drops out or jumps for short moments in an automated manual gearbox. The module sees implausible steps or brief losses that are too short or too irregular for a lasting low or high fault. Typical triggers are terminals that lose contact under vibration, a chafed harness moving with the powertrain, or moisture at the actuator connector. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Patents from Aisin AI and Nissan/Aichi show the shift stroke sensor as the feedback that confirms an engaged gear. CARB requires circuit checks on such inputs. P0914, P0916 and P0917 are the steady electrical faults of circuit A, P0915 the plausibility fault. Shifts may abort or the gearbox may briefly fall back to neutral.
Symptoms: Warning light comes and goes; Gear changes abort now and then or the gearbox drops to neutral; Fault often appears on rough roads or in wet weather
Possible Causes: Connector at the shift sensor or actuator unit losing contact under vibration (likelihood: high); Chafed or partially broken sensor wire near the gearbox (likelihood: medium); Moisture or corrosion in the connector (likelihood: medium); Shift position sensor with an internal contact or track fault (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0918 (Gear Shift Position Circuit A Intermittent). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: gear shift position sensor a, wiring harness, tcm. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-4 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Connector at the shift sensor or actuator unit losing contact under vibration (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Chafed or partially broken sensor wire near the gearbox (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Title: DTC P2701 - Transmission Friction Element B Apply Time Range/Performance
Diagnostic Codes: P2701
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: P2701 concerns friction element B: the controller has measured an apply time for this clutch or brake that falls outside its learned window. The letter is assigned per gearbox, and bulletins show how varied the causes are. Ford's SSM 47361 pairs P2701 with P0757 on the 2018 Mustang 10R80 when it will not shift beyond second gear and traces it to one-way clutch damage in the front support. On 6F50/6F55 units built from November 2015 to February 2016, SSM 46069 and 50861 combine it with P0756 and loss of reverse, third and fifth gear, caused by a displaced direct clutch snap ring. A 2023 Stellantis case for Ram Heavy Duty trucks links P2701 and harsh shifts to a dislodged 2C clutch snap ring. Expect harsh shifts, flare or a missing gear.
Symptoms: Harsh shifts or engine flare during shifts; One or more gears missing, e.g. no upshift beyond second; Warning light on
Possible Causes: Mechanical damage in clutch B, such as a displaced snap ring or damaged hub (likelihood: high); Damaged one-way clutch working together with element B (likelihood: medium); Sticking valve or pressure control solenoid for clutch B (likelihood: medium); Low or contaminated transmission fluid (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P2701 (Transmission Friction Element B Apply Time Range/Performance). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: friction element b, hydraulic control unit, pressure control solenoid. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-12 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Mechanical damage in clutch B, such as a displaced snap ring or damaged hub (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Damaged one-way clutch working together with element B (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Title: DTC P277F - Clutch B Unexpected Mechanical Gear Disengagement
Diagnostic Codes: P277F
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: P277F is the even-gear twin of P277E: the controller has found that a gear carried by the shaft of clutch B lost its engagement on its own while the car was driving through that clutch. The evidence comes from speed sensors, which show the synchronizer of the active gear turning at a different speed even though clutch B is practically locked (GM: slip below 50 rpm, 1 s confirmation, Type A in the 2023 dual-clutch TCM tables). Ford's 2024 summary assigns the code to the even clutch shaft of its TR9070 gearbox. Typical reasons are worn fork detents or engagement teeth, a shift rod that creeps because of hydraulic leakage, or a fork position learned wrongly after a repair. The even gears are then often locked out, and a relearn with a scan tool is normally part of the fix.
Symptoms: Momentary loss of drive in an even gear; Even gears unavailable, gearbox skips between odd gears; Warning lamp with stored transmission fault
Possible Causes: Worn detent or engagement teeth on an even gear or its sleeve (likelihood: high); Shift rod of the even shaft creeping due to leakage in the hydraulic unit (likelihood: medium); Wrong or missing fork position learning after repair (likelihood: medium); Implausible even-shaft speed signal (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P277F (Clutch B Unexpected Mechanical Gear Disengagement). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: dual clutch b, hydraulic actuator. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-10 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Worn detent or engagement teeth on an even gear or its sleeve (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Shift rod of the even shaft creeping due to leakage in the hydraulic unit (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

top_10.document:
Title: DTC P2C83 - Cold Start Shift Time Too Short
Diagnostic Codes: P2C83
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: California requires every part of an emission-reducing cold-start routine to be checked while it is active and its faults to be stored apart from ordinary ones. Many automatics take part in that strategy: a warm-up gearshift mode lets the engine rev further before each upshift so engine and catalyst heat faster, as a ZF patent describes. P2C83 belongs to this family. It says a shift measured during the cold-start phase was too quick – the cold-start counterpart of P0895. Whether a maker times each ratio change or how long the warm-up mode lasts is not published, and no manufacturer documents P2C83. For comparison, Saab's 1994 automatic expected each shift to take 0.3–1.3 s. Too short a shift points to excessive clutch pressure or a fill adaptation off target with cold fluid; the result is a harsh first shift.
Symptoms: Harsh or jerky first upshifts after a cold start; Engine or transmission warning lamp; Shifting returns to normal once the gearbox is warm
Possible Causes: Clutch apply pressure too high while the fluid is cold (likelihood: medium); Fill or pressure adaptation for cold fluid outside its target, e.g. after a reset or software fault (likelihood: medium); Transmission fluid temperature signal implausible, so the wrong cold-start values are used (likelihood: low); Pressure control solenoid sticking or overshooting (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P2C83 (Cold Start Shift Time Too Short). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: transmission valve body, transmission fluid, tcm. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-6 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Clutch apply pressure too high while the fluid is cold (likelihood: medium). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Fill or pressure adaptation for cold fluid outside its target, e.g. after a reset or software fault (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Title: DTC P2793 - Gear Shift Direction Circuit
Diagnostic Codes: P2793
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: P2793 covers the circuit that reports the shift direction, the fore-and-aft movement along a lane that actually engages or releases a gear, as opposed to the sideways lane choice monitored by P2790. Depending on the design, an automated manual reads it from a sensor on the shift actuator, while shift-by-wire systems may take it from the lever or a separate selector module. The controller stores the circuit fault when the signal is absent or not valid at all; signals that are present but too low or too high set P2794 or P2795. No manufacturer documents P2793 publicly with set conditions; CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires such inputs to be checked for circuit integrity. If the controller cannot tell which way the shift is going, it usually stops shifting, keeps the engaged gear and turns on the warning lamp.
Symptoms: No up- or downshifts, gearbox keeps the current gear; Selector input ignored; Warning lamp and transmission message
Possible Causes: Open circuit or poor contact at the shift direction sensor connector (likelihood: high); Failed shift direction sensor on the actuator (likelihood: medium); Faulty shift lever or selector module where it sends the signal (likelihood: medium); Transmission controller input fault (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P2793 (Gear Shift Direction Circuit). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: shift direction sensor, shifter assembly, wiring harness. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-3 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Open circuit or poor contact at the shift direction sensor connector (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Failed shift direction sensor on the actuator (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Title: DTC P2E11 - Gear Selection Actuator Position Sensor Performance
Diagnostic Codes: P2E11
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: With P2E11 the position sensor of the gear selection actuator delivers values that are electrically fine but do not fit the situation: the reading stays put although the actuator was driven, or it contradicts the gear that shaft speeds prove to be engaged. No manufacturer documents P2E11 publicly. In GM's TCM tables of 2023 for a dual-clutch box (23OBDG07) one can see how such a plausibility test works on a shift rod sensor under P2832: when speed sensors confirm an engaged gear with more than 600 N of shift force applied, yet the reading lies over 1100 µm from the learned engaged position, a Type A fault follows. Ford's DPS6 flags a comparable loss of confidence in the shift drum position, including a blocked motor, under the same P2832. Typical causes are a shifted sensor magnet, mechanical wear or lost learned values.
Symptoms: Delayed or harsh shifts, gear sometimes not engaged; Transmission warning, possibly limp mode with fixed gear; Fault may clear after a relearn procedure
Possible Causes: Learned end positions lost or outdated, e.g. after battery disconnect or part replacement (likelihood: high); Sensor magnet or sensor mounting shifted, reading offset (likelihood: medium); Wear or binding in the selection mechanism, actuator does not reach its target (likelihood: medium); Sensor characteristic drifted (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P2E11 (Gear Selection Actuator Position Sensor Performance). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: gear selection actuator position sensor, wiring harness, tcm. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-4 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Learned end positions lost or outdated, e.g. after battery disconnect or part replacement (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Sensor magnet or sensor mounting shifted, reading offset (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

top_5.excerpt: P2582 points to a speed sensor A signal that cuts out or jumps for short moments while being fine in between, so the fault may be gone by the time the vehicle reaches the workshop. Loose terminals, a cracked wire that opens under vibration or heat, a...
top_5.document:
Title: DTC P2582 - Turbocharger/Supercharger Speed Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
Diagnostic Codes: P2582
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: P2582 points to a speed sensor A signal that cuts out or jumps for short moments while being fine in between, so the fault may be gone by the time the vehicle reaches the workshop. Loose terminals, a cracked wire that opens under vibration or heat, and a sensor failing internally when hot are the usual suspects. No manufacturer publishes P2582 under its own code; PACCAR's bulletin E209 on MX-11/MX-13 engines shows how hard such dropouts are to catch - its sensor fails intermittently, yet it is logged there under P2579, and the fix is a new sensor plus a 20-second high-idle check. CARB requires the boost-control electronics to be monitored for such faults. P2578, P2580 and P2581 describe faults that persist.
Symptoms: Brief power dips that come and go; Warning lamp that may switch off again; Turbo speed trace with dropouts or spikes
Possible Causes: Loose or spread terminal in the sensor connector (likelihood: high); Wire break that opens only under vibration or heat (likelihood: medium); Speed sensor A failing when hot (likelihood: medium)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P2582 (Turbocharger/Supercharger Speed Sensor A Circuit Intermittent). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: turbo speed sensor a, sensor wiring. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-3 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Loose or spread terminal in the sensor connector (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Wire break that opens only under vibration or heat (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

top_10.title: DTC P0500 - Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit
top_10.excerpt: The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. P0500 is the general code for ...
top_10.document:
Title: DTC P0500 - Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit
Diagnostic Codes: P0500
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. P0500 is the general code for this signal. Ford checks plausibility: the car must be moving (high load, positive torque), yet the signal stays below 1–5 mph for 5 s; Ford diesels flag a missing CAN message after 0.5 s. GM's Saturn ION of 2004 used high load with below 3 mph for 6.2 s (MIL after two trips); GM's 2018 tables use P0502/P0503 instead. Cruise control is then disabled and substitute values are used.
Symptoms: Check engine light on; Speedometer dead or jumping; Cruise control not working; Automatic shifts harshly or wrongly
Possible Causes: ABS/ESP module or wheel speed sensor faulty (signal source) (likelihood: high); Output speed sensor or vehicle speed sensor faulty or dirty (metal debris on the magnet) (likelihood: high); Wire or connector open or shorted, corrosion (likelihood: medium); CAN communication fault (message missing) (likelihood: medium); Wrong tyre or axle data programmed (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0500 (Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: vehicle speed sensor, abs module, sensor wiring, engine control module. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-2 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: ABS/ESP module or wheel speed sensor faulty (signal source) (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Output speed sensor or vehicle speed sensor faulty or dirty (metal debris on the magnet) (likelihood: high). Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.

top_10.excerpt: P2514 tells you the request line between the event data recorder and the engine module sits at too high a level. The recorder, normally housed in the airbag control unit, keeps a short log of speed, pedal and brake data around a collision and fetches...
top_10.document:
Title: DTC P2514 - Event Data Recorder Request Circuit High
Diagnostic Codes: P2514
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: P2514 tells you the request line between the event data recorder and the engine module sits at too high a level. The recorder, normally housed in the airbag control unit, keeps a short log of speed, pedal and brake data around a collision and fetches engine values through this line. A high reading points to a wire chafed against a powered conductor, a missing ground on the recorder side or an input stage pulled up internally. Ford is the only maker found listing P2514, in its 2014 BOSS 302S engine module code table, marked W rather than M in the lamp column, so no check engine light is expected; voltages are not published anywhere. An open line is P2512, a line pulled down is P2513. Driving is unaffected, though crash records may lack powertrain values.
Symptoms: Code stored with no effect on driving; Possibly a wrench or service indicator instead of the check engine light
Possible Causes: Request wire chafed against a powered circuit (likelihood: high); Missing ground or unplugged connector at the airbag/recorder module (likelihood: medium); Input stage in engine or recorder module faulty (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P2514 (Event Data Recorder Request Circuit High). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: event data recorder, request wire, restraint control module. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-2 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Request wire chafed against a powered circuit (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Missing ground or unplugged connector at the airbag/recorder module (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

top_5.document:
Title: DTC P2BD2 - Exhaust Aftertreatment System A Leak
Diagnostic Codes: P2BD2
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: P2BD2 reports that the first aftertreatment line, or the only one, is not gas-tight, so exhaust escapes between engine and tailpipe or false air enters. A leak upstream of the catalysts lets untreated NOx and soot out and also confuses sensors: Foton Cummins patented a check that compares the measured aftertreatment pressure with a model value from exhaust back pressure and flags a leak beyond a limit, noting that leaks also cause urea crystals and false NOx efficiency faults. Ford describes telling a leak near the particulate filter apart from a slow catalyst sensor. CARB is studying how much such unfiltered leaks add to truck emissions. No maker documents P2BD2 publicly; P2BD3 covers system B. The driver may notice exhaust smell, ticking noises and the MIL.
Symptoms: MIL on; Exhaust smell, soot marks or ticking at a joint; Follow-up SCR or particulate filter codes
Possible Causes: Loose V-band clamp or failed gasket between aftertreatment modules (likelihood: high); Cracked exhaust pipe, flex joint or catalyst housing (likelihood: medium); Leak at a sensor, DEF injector or pressure tap mounting (likelihood: medium); Pressure sensor hose cracked, making the system look leaky (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P2BD2 (Exhaust Aftertreatment System A Leak). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: exhaust aftertreatment system a, exhaust seals. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-4 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Loose V-band clamp or failed gasket between aftertreatment modules (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Cracked exhaust pipe, flex joint or catalyst housing (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

top_5.excerpt: The second exhaust fuel doser (B) keeps passing fuel after it has been told to shut. No manufacturer documents P20D5 publicly; for the single doser A, Volvo and Mack trace the equivalent code P20CF to the fuel supply or the dosing module, and Ram fix...
top_5.document:
Title: DTC P20D5 - Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector B Stuck Open
Diagnostic Codes: P20D5
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: The second exhaust fuel doser (B) keeps passing fuel after it has been told to shut. No manufacturer documents P20D5 publicly; for the single doser A, Volvo and Mack trace the equivalent code P20CF to the fuel supply or the dosing module, and Ram fixed it on Cummins pickups with software. Detection usually relies on pressure in the doser feed line not rising again after closing, or on unexplained heat across the catalyst. Raw diesel in a hot catalyst can overheat it and causes smoke and fuel smell. CARB requires such injection faults to be caught. The stuck-closed counterpart is P20D6.
Symptoms: Check engine light on; White smoke or fuel smell; Higher fuel consumption
Possible Causes: Deposits keeping doser B from sealing (likelihood: high); Upstream shutoff valve leaking fuel through (likelihood: medium); Calibration error in the control software (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P20D5 (Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector B Stuck Open). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: aftertreatment fuel injector. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-4 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Deposits keeping doser B from sealing (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Upstream shutoff valve leaking fuel through (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Title: DTC P20CF - Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Stuck Open
Diagnostic Codes: P20CF
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: The doser that adds diesel to the exhaust for filter regeneration is judged to stay open, so fuel keeps flowing after the command to close. On Volvo and Mack trucks the nozzle sits right at the turbo outlet and is fed by an AHI module; their troubleshooting guide KC-2157 points first to the fuel supply and then to that module. For 2016 US14 trucks Mack and Volvo released software because the code logged without a confirmed fault. Ram lists P20CF on the 2025–2026 2500/3500 with the 6.7 L Cummins HO among the codes cured by a PCM update. Unburned fuel can overheat the catalyst or leave as white smoke. The opposite failure is P20D0.
Symptoms: Check engine light on; White smoke or strong fuel smell from the exhaust; Very high temperatures at catalyst and filter; Higher fuel consumption
Possible Causes: Dirt or deposits holding the doser valve off its seat (likelihood: high); Upstream shutoff or dosing module letting fuel through (likelihood: medium); Calibration error, fixed by a software update (likelihood: medium)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P20CF (Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Stuck Open). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: aftertreatment fuel injector. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-4 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Dirt or deposits holding the doser valve off its seat (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Upstream shutoff or dosing module letting fuel through (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

top_5.excerpt: Ford's 6.7 and 3.0 diesels control the air mass through the EGR valve and the intake throttle. P02ED means the measured air mass stays below target with the control at its limit – too much EGR, a throttle stuck closed or a clogged intake – for 10 s (...
top_5.document:
Title: DTC P02ED - Diesel Intake Air Flow A Control System - Low Air Flow Detected
Diagnostic Codes: P02ED
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: Ford's 6.7 and 3.0 diesels control the air mass through the EGR valve and the intake throttle. P02ED means the measured air mass stays below target with the control at its limit – too much EGR, a throttle stuck closed or a clogged intake – for 10 s (6.7) or 5 s (3.0). Typical causes are an EGR valve stuck open, a clogged air filter, a sooted throttle or a dirty mass airflow sensor. The engine lacks air: loss of power, smoke and high soot load. Other manufacturers using this code were not found.
Symptoms: Check engine light on; Lack of power; Smoke, high soot load in the filter
Possible Causes: EGR valve stuck open (likelihood: high); Air filter or intake clogged (likelihood: medium); Intake throttle stuck closed or coked (likelihood: medium); Mass airflow sensor reading too low (dirty) (likelihood: medium); Underboost or turbo fault (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P02ED (Diesel Intake Air Flow A Control System - Low Air Flow Detected). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: egr valve, diesel intake throttle valve, air filter, mass air flow sensor. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-5 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: EGR valve stuck open (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Air filter or intake clogged (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

top_5.document:
Title: DTC P24A3 - Particulate Filter Restriction - Soot Accumulation (Bank 2)
Diagnostic Codes: P24A3
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: P24A3 is the bank 2 entry for a particulate filter whose soot load, estimated from differential pressure, exhaust flow and a soot model, has climbed to the point where it noticeably restricts flow and needs a regeneration. It only appears on engines with two separate filter strands, such as some V engines. Public manufacturer documentation for this exact code is missing (the NHTSA bulletin index has no hit either), so this text leans on CARB's filter-clogging requirement and on the bank 1 equivalent P2463, which Deutz lists as a high soot load warning. The stronger level for bank 2, beyond which a normal regeneration may no longer be safe, is P243F, while ash build-up is reported separately. A long motorway drive or a workshop-initiated regeneration often clears it; repeated returns point to the cause behind the soot.
Symptoms: Particulate filter or engine warning lamp; Reduced power or slow response; Higher fuel consumption
Possible Causes: Mostly short trips so passive and active regeneration cannot finish (likelihood: high); Excess soot from injectors, EGR or boost problems (likelihood: medium); Differential pressure sensor or hoses on bank 2 giving a false high reading (likelihood: medium)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P24A3 (Particulate Filter Restriction - Soot Accumulation (Bank 2)). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: dpf b2. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-2 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Mostly short trips so passive and active regeneration cannot finish (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Excess soot from injectors, EGR or boost problems (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

top_10.title: DTC P0313 - Misfire Detected with Low Fuel
top_10.excerpt: When the tank is nearly empty the fuel pump can draw air in corners or on gradients, which causes misfires. CARB allows misfire detection to be switched off at 15 % fuel or less; some manufacturers instead report misfires detected in this state under...
top_10.document:
Title: DTC P0313 - Misfire Detected with Low Fuel
Diagnostic Codes: P0313
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: When the tank is nearly empty the fuel pump can draw air in corners or on gradients, which causes misfires. CARB allows misfire detection to be switched off at 15 % fuel or less; some manufacturers instead report misfires detected in this state under P0313 rather than P030x. Ford's normal misfire monitor runs from 15 % fuel, Saab's ME9 from 12 %; Saab's T8 sets P0313 below 5 litres with the same tests as P0300 (3 % per 1,000 revolutions, flashing light at a catalyst-damaging rate). GM petrol engines simply suspend the monitor without their own code. After refuelling the symptoms usually disappear – if not, look for a real misfire cause.
Symptoms: Check engine light on (flashing at a catalyst-damaging rate); Jerking or power loss with an almost empty tank, especially in corners or uphill; Usually no symptoms after refuelling
Possible Causes: Tank nearly empty – the fuel pump draws air (corners, gradients, braking) (likelihood: high); Actual misfire cause (ignition, injector, false air) that happened at low fuel (likelihood: medium); Weak fuel pump, clogged strainer or filter, faulty swirl pot (likelihood: medium); Fuel level sender reading too low (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0313 (Misfire Detected with Low Fuel). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: fuel pump, fuel level sensor, ignition system. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. top_10.excerpt: P2A8B means vaporizer A is not doing its job well enough, rather than reporting a wiring fault. On LPG engines this unit, also called reducer or converter, draws engine coolant heat to turn liquid gas into vapour at a steady pressure. Patent US707348...
top_10.document:
Title: DTC P2A8B - Alternative Fuel Vaporizer A Performance
Diagnostic Codes: P2A8B
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: P2A8B means vaporizer A is not doing its job well enough, rather than reporting a wiring fault. On LPG engines this unit, also called reducer or converter, draws engine coolant heat to turn liquid gas into vapour at a steady pressure. Patent US7073489B2 explains the risk: evaporation chills the converter, the chill grows with gas flow, and an underheated unit can ice up until its regulator jet blocks. The AC STAG controller manual lets the system change to gas only after the reducer has warmed up and offers a pressure correction for a poorly performing reducer that floods the engine after overrun. Detection probably compares outlet temperature and gas pressure with expected values. No vehicle manufacturer documents P2A8B publicly.
Symptoms: Check engine or gas warning lamp on; System stays on petrol longer after a cold start or falls back to petrol under load; Hesitation, rough running or stalling after coasting on gas; Frost or condensation on the vaporizer body
Possible Causes: Too little coolant reaching vaporizer A (air lock, kinked hose, thermostat stuck open) (likelihood: high); Worn diaphragm or seat in the pressure stage of vaporizer A (likelihood: medium); Oily residues from the gas clogging the vaporizer chambers (likelihood: medium); Outlet temperature sensor reading wrong but still within range (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P2A8B (Alternative Fuel Vaporizer A Performance). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: alt fuel vaporizer a, engine coolant circuit, afcm. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-4 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Too little coolant reaching vaporizer A (air lock, kinked hose, thermostat stuck open) (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Worn diaphragm or seat in the pressure stage of vaporizer A (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

top_10.document:
Title: DTC P243A - Particulate Filter Restriction - Ash Accumulation (Bank 2)
Diagnostic Codes: P243A
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: P243A is the bank 2 counterpart of P242F: the ash load in the second particulate filter has grown so large that the filter chokes the exhaust and must be cleaned or replaced. A bank 2 filter only exists where each cylinder bank of a V engine feeds its own filter strand. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Bank 1 monitoring shows how such a check works: GM's 2018 diesels judge ash by a filtered flow resistance derived from differential pressure and exhaust flow (Type A), and Deutz raises a warning once a modelled ash load limit is passed. Since ash does not burn, extra regenerations will not help and only waste fuel. If only one strand shows high back pressure or regenerates more often, the problem is confined to that side.
Symptoms: MIL or filter service message; Higher fuel consumption from frequent regenerations; Reduced power at high load
Possible Causes: Bank 2 filter full of ash after long service (likelihood: high); Oil burning on bank 2 (valve stem seals, turbo seal) adding ash (likelihood: medium); Bank 2 pressure sensor or hose reporting too much restriction (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P243A (Particulate Filter Restriction - Ash Accumulation (Bank 2)). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: dpf b2. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-4 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Bank 2 filter full of ash after long service (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Oil burning on bank 2 (valve stem seals, turbo seal) adding ash (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Title: DTC P239D - Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control System - Low Air Flow Detected
Diagnostic Codes: P239D
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: P239D is the mirror image of P239C: the measured fresh-air mass remains below target although the control loop involving the B intake throttle is already at its limit. Candidates are an EGR valve that will not close and floods the intake with exhaust gas, a B flap stuck partly shut (often together with P2395), a restricted air filter or charge-air path, a turbocharger delivering too little, or an air-mass meter reading low. No manufacturer is known to publish P239D. Ford's 2023 diesels check the same condition for their one intake throttle as P02ED, with a detection time of ten seconds on the 6.7 L engine and half that on the 3.0 L. As the engine is short of air, black smoke, rapid soot loading of the DPF and a loss of power are typical; limp mode is possible.
Symptoms: Loss of power, possibly limp mode; Black smoke; Frequent particulate filter regenerations
Possible Causes: EGR valve stuck open (likelihood: high); B throttle stuck partly closed (likelihood: medium); Clogged air filter or restricted charge-air path (likelihood: medium); Contaminated air-mass meter reading too low (likelihood: medium); Turbocharger delivering too little boost (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P239D (Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control System - Low Air Flow Detected). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: egr valve, diesel intake throttle valve, air filter, mass air flow sensor. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-5 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: EGR valve stuck open (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: B throttle stuck partly closed (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Title: DTC P236F - Cylinder 12 Combustion Performance
Diagnostic Codes: P236F
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: P236F is the ECM's verdict that combustion in cylinder 12 falls short, judged from the evaluated pressure curve rather than from a single limit. No manufacturer documents it, as no twelve-cylinder engine with cylinder pressure sensing is public. BorgWarner states that its pressure glow plug lets the controller correct, cylinder by cylinder, how much fuel is injected and when, with the measured pressure as feedback. A performance code of this type follows when that trimming has used up its range for one cylinder and the result is still off target. For diesels, CARB links combustion sensors to more demanding misfire monitoring. Worn or coked injectors, poor compression, a restricted intake or contaminated fuel are typical findings. Rough running, extra smoke and P0312 may appear alongside.
Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough running; More visible exhaust smoke
Possible Causes: Injector of cylinder 12 coked or worn (likelihood: high); Weak compression in cylinder 12 (likelihood: medium); Contaminated or poor-quality fuel (likelihood: low); Restricted intake path (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P236F (Cylinder 12 Combustion Performance). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: cylinder pressure sensor glow plug, sensor wiring, engine control module, fuel injector. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-10 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Injector of cylinder 12 coked or worn (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Weak compression in cylinder 12 (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Title: DTC P0804 - Upshift/Skip Shift Lamp Control Circuit
Diagnostic Codes: P0804
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission

Title: DTC U0039 - Vehicle Communication Bus B (+) Open
Diagnostic Codes: U0039
Vehicle System: Network And Communication
Problem Description: U0039 reports a break in the (+) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus B, which on a CAN-type network is CAN-High. Deutz assigns this code to the third CAN channel of its EMR L1 engine controller and lists it for main and secondary ECU simply as an open circuit on CAN 3, without naming the wire. On a classic high-speed CAN the interruption stays invisible to the transceiver; NXP notes that even diagnosing transceivers cannot flag a wire break, so the module infers it from partners falling silent. A fault-tolerant low-speed CAN behaves differently: NXP's TJA1055 keeps sending and receiving after a CAN-High break without spoiling frames already on the line. In practice, functions beyond the break drop out while others carry on. Look for unplugged connectors, backed-out pins and breaks near moving parts.
Symptoms: Functions of modules beyond the break unavailable; Lost-communication codes for individual modules
Possible Causes: (+) wire of Bus B broken, often at a flex point (likelihood: high); Terminal backed out or spread in a connector (likelihood: medium); Connector left open after repair work (likelihood: medium)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code U0039 (Vehicle Communication Bus B (+) Open). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: bus b wiring, module connector. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-5 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: (+) wire of Bus B broken, often at a flex point (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Terminal backed out or spread in a connector (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

top_5.document:
Title: DTC U007E - Control Module Communication Bus L Off
Diagnostic Codes: U007E
Vehicle System: Network And Communication
Problem Description: There is no public manufacturer documentation for U007E; the letter L is reserved for vehicles with a dozen or more networks. The code marks the last step of the CAN error ladder. A node stays error active while its counters are below 128 and signals faults with dominant flags; between 128 and 255 it becomes error passive and may flag errors only recessively; once transmit errors exceed 255 it goes bus off and stops sending, as Wikipedia's CAN bus article describes. U007E therefore means that a module has failed repeatedly, not once. What the driver notices depends on what the silent module controls, from a missing comfort function to warning lamps, and partner modules then store their own lost-communication codes.
Symptoms: Single comfort or assistance function missing; Partner modules report lost communication
Possible Causes: Persistent short or bad contact on Bus L (likelihood: medium); Fault inside the reporting module's CAN interface (likelihood: medium)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code U007E (Control Module Communication Bus L Off). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: bus l wiring, can transceiver. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-5 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Persistent short or bad contact on Bus L (likelihood: medium). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Fault inside the reporting module's CAN interface (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Title: DTC U0094 - Vehicle Communication Bus H (+) Open
Diagnostic Codes: U0094
Vehicle System: Network And Communication
Problem Description: U0094 reports that the (+) wire of Bus H is interrupted, CAN-High where Bus H is a CAN. No manufacturer documents U0094 publicly. How much the break matters depends on the kind of CAN. A fault-tolerant low-speed CAN up to 125 kBd, built with transceivers such as NXP's TJA1055, keeps receiving differentially with a broken CANH wire, and the chip's error output toggles only if the gap separates the sending node from the listening one, so the module may see the fault only now and then. A high-speed CAN loses the far nodes. For locating it, Nissan's chart separates a break in the main line from one in a branch to a single module, judged by the resistance and voltages measured at the diagnostic socket.
Symptoms: Single modules on Bus H not reachable; Fault appears intermittently or with movement
Possible Causes: Broken (+) wire, e.g. at a hinge or flexing harness section (likelihood: high); Terminal pushed out of a connector (likelihood: medium); Corroded splice with high resistance (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code U0094 (Vehicle Communication Bus H (+) Open). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: bus h wiring, can high wire. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-5 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Broken (+) wire, e.g. at a hinge or flexing harness section (likelihood: high). top_10.excerpt: U0039 reports a break in the (+) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus B, which on a CAN-type network is CAN-High. Deutz assigns this code to the third CAN channel of its EMR L1 engine controller and lists it for main and secondary ECU simply as an ...
top_10.document:
Title: DTC U0039 - Vehicle Communication Bus B (+) Open
Diagnostic Codes: U0039
Vehicle System: Network And Communication
Problem Description: U0039 reports a break in the (+) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus B, which on a CAN-type network is CAN-High. Deutz assigns this code to the third CAN channel of its EMR L1 engine controller and lists it for main and secondary ECU simply as an open circuit on CAN 3, without naming the wire. On a classic high-speed CAN the interruption stays invisible to the transceiver; NXP notes that even diagnosing transceivers cannot flag a wire break, so the module infers it from partners falling silent. A fault-tolerant low-speed CAN behaves differently: NXP's TJA1055 keeps sending and receiving after a CAN-High break without spoiling frames already on the line. In practice, functions beyond the break drop out while others carry on. Look for unplugged connectors, backed-out pins and breaks near moving parts.
Symptoms: Functions of modules beyond the break unavailable; Lost-communication codes for individual modules
Possible Causes: (+) wire of Bus B broken, often at a flex point (likelihood: high); Terminal backed out or spread in a connector (likelihood: medium); Connector left open after repair work (likelihood: medium)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code U0039 (Vehicle Communication Bus B (+) Open). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: bus b wiring, module connector. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-5 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: (+) wire of Bus B broken, often at a flex point (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Terminal backed out or spread in a connector (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

top_10.document:
Title: DTC U007E - Control Module Communication Bus L Off
Diagnostic Codes: U007E
Vehicle System: Network And Communication
Problem Description: There is no public manufacturer documentation for U007E; the letter L is reserved for vehicles with a dozen or more networks. The code marks the last step of the CAN error ladder. A node stays error active while its counters are below 128 and signals faults with dominant flags; between 128 and 255 it becomes error passive and may flag errors only recessively; once transmit errors exceed 255 it goes bus off and stops sending, as Wikipedia's CAN bus article describes. U007E therefore means that a module has failed repeatedly, not once. What the driver notices depends on what the silent module controls, from a missing comfort function to warning lamps, and partner modules then store their own lost-communication codes.
Symptoms: Single comfort or assistance function missing; Partner modules report lost communication
Possible Causes: Persistent short or bad contact on Bus L (likelihood: medium); Fault inside the reporting module's CAN interface (likelihood: medium)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code U007E (Control Module Communication Bus L Off). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: bus l wiring, can transceiver. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-5 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Persistent short or bad contact on Bus L (likelihood: medium). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Fault inside the reporting module's CAN interface (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Title: DTC U0094 - Vehicle Communication Bus H (+) Open
Diagnostic Codes: U0094
Vehicle System: Network And Communication
Problem Description: U0094 reports that the (+) wire of Bus H is interrupted, CAN-High where Bus H is a CAN. No manufacturer documents U0094 publicly. How much the break matters depends on the kind of CAN. A fault-tolerant low-speed CAN up to 125 kBd, built with transceivers such as NXP's TJA1055, keeps receiving differentially with a broken CANH wire, and the chip's error output toggles only if the gap separates the sending node from the listening one, so the module may see the fault only now and then. A high-speed CAN loses the far nodes. For locating it, Nissan's chart separates a break in the main line from one in a branch to a single module, judged by the resistance and voltages measured at the diagnostic socket.
Symptoms: Single modules on Bus H not reachable; Fault appears intermittently or with movement
Possible Causes: Broken (+) wire, e.g. at a hinge or flexing harness section (likelihood: high); Terminal pushed out of a connector (likelihood: medium); Corroded splice with high resistance (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code U0094 (Vehicle Communication Bus H (+) Open). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: bus h wiring, can high wire. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-5 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Broken (+) wire, e.g. at a hinge or flexing harness section (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Terminal pushed out of a connector (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

top_10.document:
Title: DTC U0066 - Vehicle Communication Bus E (+) Open
Diagnostic Codes: U0066
Vehicle System: Network And Communication
Problem Description: U0066 indicates a break in the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus E. Where Bus E is a two-wire CAN, like the infotainment CAN Audi and Volkswagen monitor under that slot, the (+) wire is CAN-High. The physical layer decides how visible the fault is. With fault-tolerant low-speed hardware, NXP's TJA1055 rides through a CAN-High interruption with drivers, termination and differential receiver left as they were, and only counts edges: once CAN-High and CAN-Low differ by four pulses, its error output goes low. A high-speed transceiver offers no such check, so modules notice only that partners beyond the break fall silent. No manufacturer documents U0066 publicly; Audi's A3 case of a badly seated contact carrier in a multi-pin connector shows how such interruptions arise.
Symptoms: Modules beyond the break, often infotainment units, unreachable; Lost-communication codes for individual modules
Possible Causes: (+) wire of Bus E broken in the harness (likelihood: high); Contact carrier or terminal not seated in a multi-pin connector (likelihood: medium); Connector left unplugged after a repair (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code U0066 (Vehicle Communication Bus E (+) Open). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: bus e wiring, module connector. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-5 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: (+) wire of Bus E broken in the harness (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Contact carrier or terminal not seated in a multi-pin connector (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

top_10.document:
Title: DTC P25C9 - Brake System Control Module B Requested MIL Illumination
Diagnostic Codes: P25C9
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: P25C9 tells the engine module that a second brake system control module, labelled B, has found an emission-relevant malfunction and wants the check engine lamp switched on. GM uses the code in its hybrid OBD tables 16OBDG01, 18OBDG01 and 19OBDG01: the engine module listens to the lamp request message from module B continuously, starting three seconds after power-up, and logs P25C9 as Type A but without its own lamp request, since the brake module already asks for the lamp. Which fault lies behind it only module B can say, so its memory is read first; a low battery or network trouble can also upset it. Brake module A reports the same situation as P25A2. As braking functions may be involved, the car should be checked soon.
Symptoms: Check engine lamp on; Brake or stability warnings at the same time
Possible Causes: Fault stored in brake system control module B (likelihood: high); Weak battery or low system voltage (likelihood: medium); Communication fault between module B and its partners (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P25C9 (Brake System Control Module B Requested MIL Illumination). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: brake control module b, communication bus. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-3 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Fault stored in brake system control module B (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Weak battery or low system voltage (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Title: DTC U047B - Invalid Data Received From Restraints System Sensor K

Title: DTC U017A - Lost Communication With Restraints System Sensor K
Diagnostic Codes: U017A
Vehicle System: Network And Communication
Problem Description: U017A is logged when restraint sensor K, the eleventh remote crash sensor, has stopped sending data to the restraints module. No manufacturer documents U017A publicly; the Chrysler Jeep lists in NHTSA file PE11-019 end at the sixth satellite. Why J2012 reserves so many slots becomes clear from supplier data: a current Bosch airbag control unit serves 12 PSI5 sensor interfaces, a premium version up to 18. Higher letters therefore belong to well-equipped vehicles, for example with rear-impact sensors, which Bosch also lists as a mounting option. After rear-end repairs or work in the boot floor, check first whether such a sensor was reconnected. Deployment that depends on sensor K may be switched off; the airbag lamp lights, the MIL stays off.

Title: DTC C0052 - Steering Wheel Position Sensor Signal A
Diagnostic Codes: C0052
Vehicle System: Brakes And Suspension
Problem Description: Covers signal A of the steering wheel position sensor. Multi-track steering-angle sensors output several phase-shifted signals (A, B, C, D) so the ESC module can reconstruct absolute angle and detect a single bad channel by cross-checking. This code is set when channel A is out of range, open, shorted or does not agree with the other channels. Ford documents C0052 together with C0053, C0054 and C0055 on 2020-2021 Police Interceptor Utility vehicles, where the codes store in the steering module if the police-package steering-wheel accessory outputs are left unwired. A fault disables stability control and sets the ABS/ESC warning lamp while base braking remains. The entry follows the SAE J2012 generic definition and multi-track steering-angle sensor design.
Symptoms: Stability control disabled; ABS/ESC warning lamp on; Implausible steering angle reading
Possible Causes: Signal A open or unconnected (likelihood: high); Steering angle sensor channel A failed (likelihood: medium); Harness or connector fault (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code C0052 (Steering Wheel Position Sensor Signal A). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: steering angle sensor. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. top_5.document:
Title: DTC P0299 - Turbocharger/Supercharger A Underboost Condition
Diagnostic Codes: P0299
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: P0299 means actual boost stays below target for a period although the control already demands more. Thresholds: GM petrol 30–55 kPa below target with the warning light in the first trip; GM diesels 10–50 kPa, two trips; Ford EcoBoost more than 4 psi (about 28 kPa) for 5 s with the wastegate already commanded fully closed; Ford diesels 30–40 kPa for 10–15 s, with a further underboost code P2263. Typical causes from manufacturer bulletins: a charge air leak, a wastegate that lost its preload or whose rod came off, a leaking bypass valve, sticking turbo vanes on diesels, and ice in the charge air cooler in winter. A faulty boost sensor can also fake underboost. Many engines then limit power.
Symptoms: Loss of power, sluggish acceleration; Limp mode, power limited; Check engine light on; Whistling or hissing from the charge air path under load
Possible Causes: Leak in the charge air path (hose off or torn, cooler leaking, clamps) (likelihood: high); Wastegate faulty (rod off, preload lost, vacuum or solenoid, diaphragm) (likelihood: high); Turbo vanes sticking or turbo worn (diesel) (likelihood: medium); Bypass valve leaking (torn diaphragm) or its control (likelihood: medium); Ice in the charge air cooler, boost sensor or connector, or software (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0299 (Turbocharger/Supercharger A Underboost Condition). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: turbocharger, wastegate, charge air hoses, boost pressure sensor a. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-6 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Leak in the charge air path (hose off or torn, cooler leaking, clamps) (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Wastegate faulty (rod off, preload lost, vacuum or solenoid, diaphragm) (likelihood: high). Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.

top_5.document:
Title: DTC P0048 - Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Circuit High
Diagnostic Codes: P0048
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: "Boost control A" is the electrically driven actuator the engine control module uses to set boost pressure: depending on the engine a pulse-width modulated solenoid or vacuum converter at the wastegate, the control valve of variable turbine vanes, or an electric actuator with position feedback. The letters A and B denote two separate actuators, for example on the low- and high-pressure turbocharger of a two-stage system, not the cylinder banks. This code is set when the voltage at the control output is too high, typically because of a short to battery voltage, so the actuator cannot be driven. Without control the actuator usually falls back to its rest position, which on most engines means low boost; depending on the design too much boost is also possible.
Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or reduced power mode; Weak acceleration, noticeable turbo lag; Overboost possible in rare cases
Possible Causes: Harness chafed, short to battery voltage (likelihood: high); Actuator coil shorted (likelihood: medium); Water in the connector (likelihood: medium); Output driver in the engine control module faulty (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0048 (Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Circuit High). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: boost control actuator a, boost control actuator wiring, engine control module. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-2.5 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Harness chafed, short to battery voltage (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Actuator coil shorted (likelihood: medium). Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.
