Title: DTC P0047 - Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Circuit Low
Diagnostic Codes: P0047
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: "Boost control A" is the electrically driven actuator the engine control module uses to set boost pressure: depending on the engine a pulse-width modulated solenoid or vacuum converter at the wastegate, the control valve of variable turbine vanes, or an electric actuator with position feedback. The letters A and B denote two separate actuators, for example on the low- and high-pressure turbocharger of a two-stage system, not the cylinder banks. This code is set when the voltage at the control output is too low, typically because of a short to ground; some manufacturers also report a missing supply this way. Without control the actuator usually falls back to its rest position, which on most engines means low boost; depending on the design too much boost is also possible.
Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or reduced power mode; Weak acceleration, noticeable turbo lag; Overboost possible in rare cases
Possible Causes: Harness chafed, short to ground (likelihood: high); Actuator coil shorted (likelihood: medium); Water in the connector (likelihood: medium); Output driver in the engine control module faulty (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0047 (Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Circuit Low). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: boost control actuator a, boost control actuator wiring, engine control module. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-2.5 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Harness chafed, short to ground (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Actuator coil shorted (likelihood: medium). Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.

Title: DTC P02CA - Turbocharger/Supercharger B Overboost Condition
Diagnostic Codes: P02CA
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: Turbocharger B is a second, separately controlled turbo – on twin-turbo or two-stage systems, or one per bank. No manufacturer using the turbo B codes was found; twin-turbo engines such as GM's 3.0 V6 and Ford's 3.5 EcoBoost report boost faults under P0234/P0299 with a shared boost sensor, so the description follows CARB and the turbo A codes. P02CA means actual boost of turbo B stays above target although the control is already lowering it; for turbo A, GM petrol engines use 20–35 kPa, Ford EcoBoost more than 4 psi over 5 s. Boost is then limited.
Symptoms: Check engine light, reduced power, limp mode; Power cut under load; Possibly knocking (petrol)
Possible Causes: Wastegate B stuck closed, linkage seized (likelihood: high); Boost control valve or actuator B faulty, vacuum line swapped or leaking (likelihood: medium); Boost sensor reading wrong (likelihood: medium); Turbo B vanes sooted (diesel) (likelihood: medium); Software or calibration, tuning (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P02CA (Turbocharger/Supercharger B Overboost Condition). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: turbocharger b, wastegate b, boost control valve. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-6 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Wastegate B stuck closed, linkage seized (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Boost control valve or actuator B faulty, vacuum line swapped or leaking (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

top_10.document:
Title: DTC P0299 - Turbocharger/Supercharger A Underboost Condition
Diagnostic Codes: P0299
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: P0299 means actual boost stays below target for a period although the control already demands more. Thresholds: GM petrol 30–55 kPa below target with the warning light in the first trip; GM diesels 10–50 kPa, two trips; Ford EcoBoost more than 4 psi (about 28 kPa) for 5 s with the wastegate already commanded fully closed; Ford diesels 30–40 kPa for 10–15 s, with a further underboost code P2263. Typical causes from manufacturer bulletins: a charge air leak, a wastegate that lost its preload or whose rod came off, a leaking bypass valve, sticking turbo vanes on diesels, and ice in the charge air cooler in winter. A faulty boost sensor can also fake underboost. Many engines then limit power.
Symptoms: Loss of power, sluggish acceleration; Limp mode, power limited; Check engine light on; Whistling or hissing from the charge air path under load
Possible Causes: Leak in the charge air path (hose off or torn, cooler leaking, clamps) (likelihood: high); Wastegate faulty (rod off, preload lost, vacuum or solenoid, diaphragm) (likelihood: high); Turbo vanes sticking or turbo worn (diesel) (likelihood: medium); Bypass valve leaking (torn diaphragm) or its control (likelihood: medium); Ice in the charge air cooler, boost sensor or connector, or software (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0299 (Turbocharger/Supercharger A Underboost Condition). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: turbocharger, wastegate, charge air hoses, boost pressure sensor a. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-6 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Leak in the charge air path (hose off or torn, cooler leaking, clamps) (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Wastegate faulty (rod off, preload lost, vacuum or solenoid, diaphragm) (likelihood: high). Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.

Title: DTC P0046 - Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Circuit Range/Performance
Diagnostic Codes: P0046
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: "Boost control A" is the electrically driven actuator the engine control module uses to set boost pressure: depending on the engine a pulse-width modulated solenoid or vacuum converter at the wastegate, the control valve of variable turbine vanes, or an electric actuator with position feedback. The letters A and B denote two separate actuators, for example on the low- and high-pressure turbocharger of a two-stage system, not the cylinder banks. With this code the circuit is electrically intact, but the actuator does not follow the command plausibly: its actual position deviates too far or too long from the target, or its learned values do not fit. Boost is then too low or too high depending on where it sticks, often with reduced power.
Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or reduced power mode; Weak acceleration, noticeable turbo lag; Overboost possible in rare cases
Possible Causes: Turbine vanes or wastegate linkage sooted or sticking (likelihood: high); Electric actuator faulty (likelihood: high); Actuator learn value invalid, e.g. after low battery voltage at start (likelihood: medium); Vacuum leak at a pneumatic actuator (likelihood: medium); Actuator position sensor faulty (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0046 (Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Circuit Range/Performance). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: boost control actuator a, turbocharger, actuator position sensor. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-4 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Turbine vanes or wastegate linkage sooted or sticking (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Electric actuator faulty (likelihood: high). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Title: DTC P0049 - Turbocharger/Supercharger A Turbine Overspeed
Diagnostic Codes: P0049
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: The control module has detected that turbocharger A runs above its permitted maximum speed. Engines equipped for it measure turbine speed with a dedicated sensor on the shaft; while the fault is active some systems continue with an estimated speed and reduce power. Real overspeed arises when too much exhaust energy reaches the turbine, for example because the wastegate or the turbine vanes stick closed, or because the turbocharger has to compensate for a charge-air leak or high altitude. Since a damaged turbocharger can fail completely, the cause should be found before driving on. Turbocharger B has its own code.
Symptoms: Check engine light on; Reduced power or limp mode; Whistling from the turbocharger; Risk of turbocharger damage
Possible Causes: Wastegate or turbine vanes stuck closed, boost control fails (likelihood: medium); Turbocharger speed sensor or its wiring faulty (likelihood: medium); Charge-air leak forcing the turbocharger to higher speed (likelihood: low); Engine control module or software (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0049 (Turbocharger/Supercharger A Turbine Overspeed). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: turbocharger, turbocharger speed sensor, wastegate, turbocharger vanes or wastegate. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-5 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Wastegate or turbine vanes stuck closed, boost control fails (likelihood: medium). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Turbocharger speed sensor or its wiring faulty (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Title: DTC P226B - Turbocharger/Supercharger A Boost Pressure Too High - Mechanical
Diagnostic Codes: P226B
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: P226B reports boost from turbocharger or supercharger A rising too high for a mechanical reason, for instance a wastegate or bypass that will not open or a seized actuator linkage, rather than a sensor or wiring fault. VW's 2014 book for the supercharged Touareg 3.0 TSI sets it when boost passes 250 kPa. GM uses the code only for European calibrations: its 2018 diesel tables list P226B as an EOBD code in the boost-system fault groups, while the US software maps the same fault group to P2263. CARB requires boosted engines to detect overboost. Where P0234 judges a deviation above the target, P226B points to a mechanical cause; P2262 describes boost that does not appear at all. To protect the engine the ECM usually reduces torque, and some engines open a relief path.
Symptoms: Sudden power cut or reduced-power mode under load; MIL on; Unusually strong surge of power just before the cut
Possible Causes: Wastegate flap seized closed by corrosion or carbon (likelihood: high); Seized or misadjusted wastegate or VGT actuator linkage (likelihood: medium); Vacuum or pressure line to a pneumatic actuator leaking or blocked (likelihood: medium); Supercharger bypass valve not opening (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P226B (Turbocharger/Supercharger A Boost Pressure Too High - Mechanical). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: turbocharger, wastegate, wastegate actuator. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-6 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Wastegate flap seized closed by corrosion or carbon (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Seized or misadjusted wastegate or VGT actuator linkage (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Problem Description: P2263 means boost pressure measured in the intake manifold stays too far from the target set by the closed-loop boost control. CARB requires diesel OBD to detect underboost, overboost and slow response of the boost control. On the 2014 Cruze 2.0 diesel the allowed underboost deviation runs from 35 to 85 kPa with injection quantity and speed, and the code sets as Type A once the condition holds for 15 s; GM's 2018 diesels need 400 failures in 500 samples and name leaks after the compressor or in the manifolds, and exhaust obstructions, as targets. Ford's 2023 diesels count deviations above 35 kPa at 1500 rpm or more, typically over 100 s. The Opel/GM 2.0 CDTi in the Saab 9-5 (2010) waits for more than 200 s out of range and stores it as Type C. GM's Cruze bulletin found a charge-air cooler duct pulled off the throttle body, with P0299, P2002 and P2463 alongside. The engine usually limits torque.
Symptoms: Power loss or limp mode; Hissing or whistling from the charge-air system; Black smoke under load
Possible Causes: Charge-air hose or cooler duct leaking or pulled off (likelihood: high); Variable-geometry vanes or actuator sticking (likelihood: medium); Restricted exhaust, for example a heavily loaded particulate filter (likelihood: low); Boost pressure sensor reading wrong (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P2263 (Turbocharger/Supercharger A Boost System Performance). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: turbocharger, vnt actuator, charge air pipe, charge air cooler, boost pressure sensor. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-6 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Charge-air hose or cooler duct leaking or pulled off (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Variable-geometry vanes or actuator sticking (likelihood: medium). Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

Title: DTC P005F - Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control B Supply Voltage Circuit High
Diagnostic Codes: P005F
Vehicle System: Engine And Transmission
Problem Description: "Boost control B" is the electrically driven actuator the engine control module uses to set boost pressure: depending on the engine a pulse-width modulated solenoid or vacuum converter at the wastegate, the control valve of variable turbine vanes, or an electric actuator with position feedback. B is the second actuator, for example on the high-pressure turbocharger of a two-stage system or on the second turbocharger; it does not denote cylinder bank 2. This code concerns the supply voltage that the control module switches to the actuator (high side): it is too high, for example because of a short to battery voltage. Without control the actuator usually falls back to its rest position, which on most engines means low boost; depending on the design too much boost is also possible.
Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or reduced power mode; Weak acceleration, noticeable turbo lag; Overboost possible in rare cases
Possible Causes: Supply wire shorted to battery voltage (likelihood: high); Water or corrosion in the connector (likelihood: medium); Internal fault in the actuator (likelihood: medium); High-side driver in the engine control module faulty (likelihood: low)
Diagnostic Steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P005F (Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control B Supply Voltage Circuit High). Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: boost control actuator b, boost control actuator wiring, engine control module. Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement. Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications. Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-2.5 hours
Recommended Actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Supply wire shorted to battery voltage (likelihood: high). If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Water or corrosion in the connector (likelihood: medium). Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.
